title: Febrile seizures | NHS inform
text:
Febrile seizures
A febrile seizure is a convulsion (also known as a fit) that can happen when a child has a
fever
. Febrile seizures are also sometimes called febrile convulsions.
Febrile seizures are quite common and aren’t usually serious. Most children make a full recovery afterwards.
Phone 999 or go to A&E if:
your child is having difficulty breathing
this is your child’s first seizure
the seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes
Phone 111 if:
your child has had febrile seizures before
the seizure lasts less than 5 minutes
your child has signs of dehydration like sunken eyes, dry mouth or no tears when they cry
What to do during a seizure
If a child is having a febrile seizure, place them in the
recovery position
. To do this:
Lay them on their side, on a soft surface.
Turn their face to one side.
This will stop them swallowing any vomit, keep their airway open and help prevent injury.
Stay with your child and try to make a note of how long the seizure lasts.
Don’t put anything, including medication, in your child’s mouth during a seizure.
There’s a small chance that they might bite their tongue.
Symptoms of febrile seizures
The main symptom of a febrile seizure is a convulsion that happens while a child has a fever. A high fever is usually 38C (100.4F) or above.
Febrile seizures often occur during the first day of a fever. However, there’s no connection between how high the fever is and the start of a seizure. Seizures can happen even when a child has a mild fever.
There are 2 main types of febrile seizure. These are simple febrile seizure and complex febrile seizure.
Simple febrile seizure
During a simple febrile seizure, your child may:
become stiff
twitch their arms and legs
lose consciousness
wet or soil themselves
vomit or foam at the mouth
roll their eyes back
The seizure usually lasts less than 5 minutes but can last up to 15 minutes. After the seizure, your child may be sleepy for up to an hour.
A simple febrile seizure doesn’t happen again within 24 hours or in the period of your child’s illness.
Complex febrile seizure
Complex febrile seizures are less common.
A complex febrile seizure can:
last longer than 15 minutes
cause symptoms that only affect one area of the body
happen again within 24 hours
happen again during your child’s illness
Your child may not fully recover from a complex febrile seizure within one hour.
Diagnosing febrile seizures
Febrile seizures can often be diagnosed if you give healthcare professionals a description of what happened.
It’s useful to know:
how long the seizure lasted
what happened
if your child recovered within an hour
if your child has had a seizure before
Sometimes your child may need extra tests to help find out the reason for their seizures.
Treatment for febrile seizures
Often febrile seizures don’t need any specific treatments.
If the seizures are caused by a high temperature, lowering this can make your child feel more comfortable.
Children’s
paracetamol
and
ibuprofen
can help to lower a high temperature. They work as antipyretics, which help to reduce fever, as well as being painkillers. You can’t give them both at the same time, but if one doesn’t work, you may want to try the other later.
It may also help to remove unnecessary clothing and bedding to help reduce your child’s temperature.
It’s important to prevent
dehydration
during a fever. To do this, make sure your child drinks plenty of fluids.
Your healthcare professional can give you more advice about treating a high temperature.
Further information on fever in children
Managing a fever in children
Watch this video for more advice on how to manage a fever in children, including self-care and when to get help.
What causes febrile seizures?
It’s not known exactly what causes febrile seizures, but they’re linked to a rise in temperature.
A high temperature can be caused by infections like:
chickenpox
flu
middle ear infections
tonsilitis
a urinary tract infection (UTI)
Febrile seizures can also happen when a child’s temperature drops from a high level.
Having a family history of febrile seizures may increase the chances of having one.
In rare cases, febrile seizures can happen after a child has a vaccination.
Who’s most at risk of febrile seizures
Febrile seizures are most likely between the age of 6 months and 3 years.
Complications of febrile seizures
Children who have had complex febrile seizures have a small chance of developing
epilepsy
.
